title: Read and make bar graphs and pictographs where one unit stands for one

lesson.title: One Square, One Thing: Making a Bar Graph

steps.say: You already know how to count things and write the number in a table. Today we learn one small step: turning those counts into a bar graph where one square on the graph stands for one thing.

visual.caption: Our class picked a favourite fruit. This table shows how many chose each one.

steps.say: Here is the rule for this kind of graph: one square equals one person. So the apple bar climbs up five squares, because five kids picked apples. The blueberry bar climbs up three squares. Count the squares, and you get the number back.

visual.caption: Each bar starts at zero and climbs one square for each student.

steps.say: Let us build the orange bar together, step by step. First, find the word Oranges at the bottom. Next, look in the table: four students. Then start at zero and colour one square, two squares, three squares, four squares. Stop. The top of the bar lands right on the four. That is why it works, because every square you coloured was one real student.

visual.caption: Colour up one square at a time until you have four.

steps.say: Now let us read the graph instead of building it. Which fruit won? Apples, because that bar is the tallest at five. How many more kids picked apples than bananas? Apples is five, bananas is two, and five take away two is three. So three more kids picked apples.

visual.caption: Five squares next to two squares. The difference is three squares.

steps.say: Here is a mistake lots of kids make. They count the lines on the graph paper instead of the squares, so a bar of three gets called four. Watch out for this. Always start counting at zero, which is the bottom line, and count the spaces you coloured, not the lines. Three coloured squares means three students, every time.

visual.caption: Count the coloured squares, not the lines. This bar is three, not four.

steps.say: So remember, when one square stands for one thing, the height of the bar simply is the number. Count squares up from zero, and the graph tells you the answer.

lesson.answer: One square equals one thing, so count squares up from zero and the bar's height is the number.

practice.question: At a Saturday farmers market in Kelowna, a stand sold six loaves of bread, four jars of honey, seven bags of apples, and three bunches of carrots. On graph paper, draw a bar graph where one square stands for one item sold. Which bar is the tallest, and how many more bags of apples were sold than bunches of carrots?
practice.answer: The bars go up six, four, seven, and three squares. The apple bar is the tallest at seven squares, and seven take away three is four, so four more bags of apples were sold than bunches of carrots.
